full_judgment:
2. Material facts are these. On 25 May 1994 the plaintiff-respondents numbering 18 instituted in the First Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong a suit being Other Class Suit No.98 of 1994 against the defendant-petitioners praying for a declaratory judgment that the notice for 

 their eviction from the disputed shops as contained in Memo No.AE0/395- Commercial/ Station Road/ Chittagong dated 19 May 1994 signed by defendant No. 3 Deputy Commissioner (Land & Building) Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong is illegal and not binding upon them. A further prayer was made for permanent injunction restraining the defendant-petitioners from dispossessing them from the suit premises. On the same day the plaintiff-respondents made an application for temporary injunction whereupon notices were issued to the defendant-petitioners to show cause why the prayer for temporary injunction should not be allowed. On 9 August 1994 the defendant-petitioners entered appearance in the suit and prayed for time to file written objection which was allowed till 1 September 1994. In the meantime the defendant-petitioners locked the shops in suit on 17 August 1994. The plaintiff-respondents thereafter came up with an application on 18 August 1994 for mandatory injunction directing the defendant-petitioners to unlock the shops. Pursuant to a notice of the Court the defendant-petitioners filed a written objection thereto contending that they had locked the shops as the plaintiff-respondents became trespassers in consequence of the cancellation of their licence for violation of the terms and non-renewal 1993. By an order dated 30 August 1994 the learned Assistant Judge allowed the prayer for mandatory injunction and directed the defendant-petitioners to unlock the shops by 1 September 1994. The defendant-petitioners went up in appeal to the learned District Judge, Chittagong who admitted the appeal and refused to stay the operation of the order of mandatory injunction. Being aggrieved the plaintiff-respondents preferred Civil Revision No. 3106 of 1994 calling in question the maintainability of the appeal. The defendant-petitioners also preferred Civil Revision No. 3337 of 1994 against the order of refusal to stay. By a common order dated 12 July 1995 a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division set aside the order admitting the appeal and also the order of the trial court granting mandatory injunction. He further directed the trial court to hear the application for temporary injunction and mandatory injunction together. After the remand the learned Assistant Judge, Chittagong allowed the prayers for mandatory injunction as also temporary injunction by his order dated 21 November 1995. Against this order the defendant-petitioners filed Civil Revision No. 4863 of 1995 to the High Court Division which discharged the Rule by the impugned order. 

 3. Mr. Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioners argues that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was wrong in refusing to set aside the order granting mandatory and preventive injunction on the facts and in the circumstances of the case inasmuch as the learned Judge failed to notice that the plaintiffs had no subsisting legal right in the shops in question as their licence were cancelled and those had not been renewed. 

 4. It appears that on consideration of the facts of the case the trial court was satisfied that the plaintiff-respondents succeeded in making out a prima facie case for injunction in respect of the disputed shops and that the locking of the same by the defendant-petitioners was contrary to equity and justice. The High Court Division also noticed that the defendant-petitioners received the notice of the, application for injunction and pre-empted the plaintiff-respondents in order to forestall all possible orders of the courts in favour of the plaintiffs. In such a situation  this court had already held in Abdul Jalil Munshi and Another Vs. Abu Bakar Siddique, 35 DLR (AD) 42 that a mandatory injunction was justified we have nothing to depart from this view. The learned Counsel for the petitioners could not also show that the judgment of the High Court 'Division suffers from any legal infirmity calling for our interference.
